title: Concurrency Overview: GIL, Threading, Multiprocessing, and Asyncio
description: A conceptual overview of Python's approaches to concurrency and the Global Interpreter Lock's effect on them.
objectives: Understand the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) and its practical effect
Distinguish threading, multiprocessing, and asyncio at a conceptual level
Know which approach suits which kind of workload

content.heading: The GIL and Threading
content.body: The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is a mutex in CPython that ensures only one thread executes Python bytecode at any given instant, even on a multi-core machine. This means Python threads (the threading module) do not achieve true parallel speedup for CPU-bound work — two threads doing pure computation will not run meaningfully faster than one, since they take turns holding the GIL. Threads are, however, genuinely useful for I/O-bound work (network requests, file I/O, waiting on a database): while one thread is blocked waiting on I/O, it releases the GIL, letting another thread run — this is where threading shines in Python.

content.heading: Multiprocessing and Asyncio
content.body:
The multiprocessing module sidesteps the GIL entirely by running separate Python processes, each with its own interpreter and memory space (communicating via pickling and inter-process channels), achieving true parallelism for CPU-bound work at the cost of higher memory usage and slower inter-process communication than threads sharing memory directly.

asyncio offers a third model: a single-threaded event loop running many cooperative coroutines (functions defined with async def, calling other coroutines with await), switching between them whenever one is waiting on I/O. It avoids both the GIL contention of threads and the overhead of separate processes, but requires 'async-aware' libraries throughout and a mental model shift (cooperative yielding, not preemptive interruption). As a rule of thumb: use threading or asyncio for I/O-bound work, and multiprocessing for CPU-bound work that needs true parallelism.

content.code:
import threading

def worker(n):
    total = sum(range(n))   # CPU-bound — GIL limits real parallel speedup here
    print(total)

threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(1000000,)) for _ in range(2)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

# Conceptual sketch of asyncio (not executed here):
# async def fetch(url): ...
# async def main():
#     await asyncio.gather(fetch(url1), fetch(url2))
content.explanation: The threading example is CPU-bound, so the GIL prevents the two threads from truly running in parallel — this workload would benefit more from multiprocessing. The asyncio sketch shows the cooperative-coroutine style used for I/O-bound concurrency.

keyPoints: The GIL means only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time in CPython
threading helps with I/O-bound work (waiting releases the GIL); it does not speed up pure CPU-bound work
multiprocessing achieves true parallelism for CPU-bound work by using separate processes, each with its own GIL
asyncio provides single-threaded, cooperative concurrency ideal for many simultaneous I/O-bound tasks
commonMistakes: Using threading for CPU-bound work and being surprised it isn't faster
Using multiprocessing for lightweight I/O-bound tasks, paying unnecessary process-startup and IPC overhead
Mixing blocking (synchronous) calls inside asyncio coroutines, which stalls the entire single-threaded event loop
